result: The authors developed a zebrafish glioblastoma model (p53EPS) by co-injecting linearized her4.1:EGFRvIII, her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R, and her4.1:mScarlet transgenes into tp53-/- embryos, resulting in visible brain lesions by 15 dpf with 15-20% tumor incidence by 45 dpf. Tumors expressed glial markers (gfap:EGFP) and were transplantable, demonstrating oncogenic transformation.
evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the model generation. Reviewer 3 states the authors "convincingly show that co-injection of activated human EGFRviii, PI3KCAH1047R, and mScarlet into TP53 null zebrafish promotes formation of fluorescent brain lesions and glioblastoma-like tumor formation." Reviewer 2 notes "the authors have generated a novel glioblastoma model in zebrafish" as a key strength. No concerns were raised about these foundational claims.

result: Histological characterization revealed p53EPS tumors display aggressive and proliferative features with heterogeneous cell types (round granular and flattened elongated morphologies), embryonal features including rosette structures, and increased p-ERK and p-AKT staining. Tumors generally showed clean margins without invasive boundaries, necrosis, or microvascular proliferation.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states "The authors include histological characterization of the tumors, as well as quantifications of p-ERK and p-AKT staining to highlight increased activation of the MAPK/AKT signaling pathways." Reviewer 2 initially requested more histologic characterization but later noted in an update: "The more detailed description of the tumour histology is very interesting and the authors have addressed my previous concerns nicely." This indicates the histological claims are now accepted.

result: Gene expression analysis showed p53EPS tumors significantly enrich for the mesenchymal subtype of human glioblastoma, with no significant enrichment for other glioblastoma or medulloblastoma subtypes.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a conceptual concern: "EGFRvIII is mainly associated with the classical subtype, so the mesenchymal subtype might be unexpected here. This could be commented on." While the data showing mesenchymal enrichment is not directly challenged, the reviewer questions whether this finding aligns with expectations given the genetic drivers used, suggesting the interpretation may require additional context or explanation.

result: p53EPS tumors display a strong inflammatory component with enrichment for inflammation-related pathways (interferon gamma response, TNFA signaling, interferon alpha response, JAK/STAT3 signaling) and increased immune cell and inflammatory gene expression in both tumor and stromal cell fractions.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 states the authors "identified gene expression patterns associated with inflammation" and notes this as part of the study's contributions. The editor describes the data as "compelling" and notes the model opens "new lines of inquiries for future investigation." No reviewer challenges the inflammatory signature findings.

result: Live imaging revealed phagocytic cell infiltration into early-stage p53EPS lesions, with neutral red-positive phagocytes and tnfa:EGFP+ activated phagocytes enriched in tumor regions. Time-course analysis showed mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages consistently associated with tumor lesions by 7-9 dpf.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 states "Live imaging revealed high levels of immune cell infiltration and associations between microglia/macrophages and tumor cells" and notes "Quantification of the emergence of macrophages over time in relation to tumor initiation and growth is provided and supports the observations." Reviewer 2 describes "Video 1 was very impressive in my opinion and shows the model is a very useful tool to study microglia/macrophage:glioblastoma cell interactions."

result: mpeg1.1:EGFP+ microglia/macrophages displayed morphological changes (from ramified to amoeboid) and internalized her4.1:mScarlet+ tumor cells, suggesting phagocytosis of tumor cells during early tumor formation.
evaluation: While Reviewer 2 praises the visualization ("Video 1 was very impressive") and Reviewer 3 notes the authors "nicely show high levels of immune cell infiltration," Reviewer 2 raises an important interpretive concern: "Phagocytosis could have antitumour effects through removal of live cancer cells, or could be cancer promoting if apoptotic cancer cells are being rapidly cleared with concomitant activation of an immunosuppressive phenotype in the phagocytes (i.e. efferocytosis). It may be possible to distinguish between these two types of phagocytosis experimentally." This suggests uncertainty about the functional interpretation of the phagocytosis observations.

result: Gene set enrichment analysis showed p53EPS tissues more significantly enrich for M1 (pro-inflammatory) macrophage signatures compared to M2 (alternative) polarized macrophage signatures.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly challenges the M1/M2 framework: "Current thinking in established human glioblastoma is that the M1/M2 designations for macrophages are not relevant, with microglia macrophage populations showing a mixture of pre- and anti-inflammatory features. Ideally there would be a much more detailed characterization of the intratumoral microglia/macrophage population here, as single markers can't be relied upon." This indicates the reviewer questions whether the M1/M2 classification is appropriate for interpreting these data.

result: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockdown of inflammatory transcription factors irf7 or irf8 led to increased p53EPS tumor formation (65% for irf7, 42% for irf8, compared to 20% control), suggesting pro-inflammatory cell types exert negative regulatory pressure on tumor growth at early stages.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states "The irf7/irf8 knockdown and the chlodronate experiments are consistent with a role for mature myeloid cells in suppressing tumour initiation." Reviewer 3 notes "the authors provide evidence for key genetic regulators of the local microenvironment, showing increased p53EPS tumor initiation following Ifr7 gene knock-down." However, Reviewer 2 asks: "Do the irf7/8 and chlodronate experiments distinguish between effects on microglia/macrophages and dendritic cells?" suggesting some uncertainty about cell-type specificity.

result: Tumor cell-specific knockdown of irf7 or irf8 using Tg(her4.1:Cas9-2A-EGFP) did not significantly change p53EPS tumor formation, suggesting the tumor-suppressive effects of irf7/irf8 act through the tumor microenvironment rather than tumor cells themselves.
evaluation: This mechanistic distinction is not explicitly discussed by reviewers, but the overall irf7/irf8 findings are accepted (see above). The cell-type-specific experiments support the interpretation that effects are TME-mediated, which aligns with reviewer acceptance of the broader immune surveillance findings.

result: Suppression of phagocyte activity through Clodronate liposomes (50% vs 23% engraftment) or irf8 knockdown in host zebrafish (46% vs 19% engraftment) led to enhanced p53EPS tumor cell engraftment following transplantation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states "The irf7/irf8 knockdown and the chlodronate experiments are consistent with a role for mature myeloid cells in suppressing tumour initiation." Reviewer 3 notes "experiments to deplete the macrophages using clodronate liposomes suggest that macrophages contribute to the suppression of tumor engraftment following transplantation." The editor describes the data as "compelling."

result: Co-injection of her4.1:KRASG12D + her4.1:PI3KCAH1047R + her4.1:EGFP (p53KPG) resulted in tumor onset and penetrance comparable to p53EPS, suggesting MAPK/AKT pathway activation plays a dominant role in driving tumor formation downstream of RTK signaling.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the authors use "a transplantation assay to further test the tumorigenic potential of dissociated cells from glial-derived tumors" and describes the model validation positively. No reviewer challenges the KRAS-driven model or the interpretation about pathway dominance.

result: The innate immune system plays important tumor-suppressive roles during glioblastoma initiation, as demonstrated through live imaging, CRISPR-mediated gene targeting, and transplantation experiments.
evaluation: This overarching conclusion is supported by multiple reviewer statements. Reviewer 2 notes the model "may also be very valuable in understanding immune surveillance in glioblastoma initiation." Reviewer 3 states the results "provide new insights into the regulation of glioblastoma initiation and growth by the surrounding microenvironment." The editor calls the study "valuable" and the data "compelling."
